title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
hookLine: a sinful woman washes his feet with tears at a dinner she wasn't invited to

lines: AN UNINVITED WOMAN WITH A JAR.
cards: A dinner party in a nice house. The host is a Pharisee named Simon, who has asked the new teacher everyone is talking about to eat with him.
The guests aren't on chairs; they recline on couches, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them.
And someone comes in who was never asked: a woman of the city, known as a sinner, carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. She goes straight to the teacher's feet.

teach.b: She stands behind him and starts to cry. Her tears fall on his feet, so she wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out the ointment.
Simon thinks: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what sort of woman is touching him. Jesus answers the thought with a story. Two men owe a lender money, one five hundred pence, one fifty.
Neither can pay, so he forgives them both. Which will love him more? Simon answers carefully: I suppose the one forgiven more.
Right, says Jesus. Then he turns toward the woman but keeps talking to Simon. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears.
You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet.
Then the line: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loveth less."

teach.h: NO WATER, NO KISS, NO OIL.
teach.b: To her he says: "Thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace."
Simon isn't the villain here. He invited Jesus, listened, and answered honestly. The story is about two kinds of guests, and it asks which one we are.
Luke never names the woman. For many centuries in the Western Church, following a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was identified with Mary Magdalene.
The Church's calendar today no longer joins them, and the Gospel itself never says.
What Luke does say is that she loved much, and that Jesus sent her away forgiven, in peace.

how: Catholics connect this story with the sacrament of Penance, where sins are forgiven and the priest sends the penitent away in peace, and some pray with it as an examination of how much they have been forgiven.

games.q: you're the host. an uninvited woman with a bad reputation is weeping on your guest's feet. what do you think?
o: if he were a prophet, he'd know what she is.
she's showing the welcome I forgot to give.
someone should ask her to leave.
games.why: Simon thinks the first. Jesus answers with a story, then shows him the second was true: no water, no kiss, no oil from the host.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been forgiven, by God if you pray, or by a friend, a parent, a partner who let something go, and remember how it felt when they didn't hold it over you.

Then think of one person you've been loving carefully, in measured amounts, keeping track, and picture giving them one thing without counting: a kindness, an apology, an hour. If you pray, thank God for what you've been forgiven.

wordCard.voice: Alabaster. The jar of ointment the unnamed woman poured on Jesus' feet at Simon's dinner, her tears showing how much she knew she'd been forgiven. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: she loved much. The verb is the agape word, love that gives.

carryVoice: Your line: go in peace. She was forgiven much, and she loved much. See you tomorrow.
